Details

DESCRIPTION

Simulate population of individual-level data and fit Bayesian GLMMs using different software.

INPUTS

(None)

OUTPUTS

Model estimates.

Motivation

Bayesian modelling represents a flexible and robust aproach to statistical modelling. Multiple software interfaces make it possible for the user to define models at a high level of abstraction, that can then be converted to more explicit code that runs efficiently within a Hamiltonian Markov-chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) procedure using a No U-Turns Sampler (NUTS) on various operating systems.

In R the brms package allows users to define models that can then be run as C++ executables by rstan (default) or cmdstanr (faster). In Python the Bambi package performs the same role for generating PyMC models, which rely on numpyro and JAX for sampling. Nutpie executes sampling via the extremely efficient Rust programming language, and can be used to sample (most) models written in PyMC or Stan. It also uses a very stable Hamiltonian MCMC algorithm (Seyboldt et al.), which seems to improve chain convergence and reduce the rate of divergent transitions; both of which reduce the reliability of model estimates.

Set up workspace

To make use of Python via R, make sure that reticulate, posterior and bayesplot, are installed, and (on Windows) that you have installed the latest version of Rtools. Here we first set up a reticulate Python environment with the appropriate versions of each package, then load reticulate to ensure that those packages are available. We then load the packages required for brms models: brms, rstan and cmdstanr.

Simuluate some data

Simulate data from a random binomial

set.seed(17070523)#seed the random number generator with Linnaeus' birthday


# . Set up simulation parameters ------------------------------------------

#Experimental variables
n_animals = 10# number of individuals
n_levels = 7# number of stimulus levels per individual
n_types = 2# number of stimulus types
replicates = 20#number of replicates of each condition

#starting parameters
pop_mean = 5.00#population mean
pop_sd = 1.00#population standard deviation
slope_mean = 3.00#population slope
slope_sd = 1.03#population slope standard deviation
type_mean = 2.50# effect of stimulus type 2 on average response
type_slope = 3.5# effect of type 2 on response to stimulus intensity
type_animal_sd = 0.55# sd of effect of animal on effect of type 2
extra_error_sd = 0.10#small source of unaccounted error


# . Set up experimental design --------------------------------------------

#Experiment design
animal = rep(x = 1:n_animals, # each animal has a number and experiences each level
             times = n_levels)
animal = sort(animal)# vector of animal numbers organised in order
animal = rep(x = animal, # each animal and level also includes each type
             times = n_types)
stimulus = rep(x = 1:n_levels - 1,# each stimulus has a number and repeats for each animal
               times = n_animals)
stimulus = rep(x = stimulus, # repeat stimulus for each type
               times = n_types)
stype = rep(x = 1:n_types, # each stimulus type for each animal and number
            times = n_animals * n_levels)
stype = sort(stype) # arrange in order

#replicate each observation
animal = rep(x = animal,
             times = replicates)
stimulus = rep(x = stimulus,
               times = replicates)
stype = rep(x = stype,
            times = replicates)

#baseline bias (response when stimulus = 0 and type = 1)
base_bias_animal = rnorm(n = n_animals,
                         mean  = pop_mean,
                         sd = pop_sd)
#response increase with each stimulus level
slope_animal = rnorm(n = n_animals,
                     mean = slope_mean,
                     sd = slope_sd)
#response to type 2
type_animal = rnorm(n = n_animals,
                    mean = 1.0, # on average, no random effect
                    sd = type_animal_sd)

# . Generate simulated data -----------------------------------------------

#Make an empty vector
response_y = rep(x = NA,
                 length = n_animals * n_levels * n_types * replicates)
#Loop through experiment design and generate theoretical response
for (ii in 1:length(response_y))
{
  #each data point is generated from the animal's intercept
  #plus the effect of stimulus type
  #plus the animal's response (slope) to changing stimulus level
  #scaled by the effect of different stimlus types
  #plus a small additional source or error
  response_y[ii] = base_bias_animal[animal[ii]] +
    (stype[ii] - 1) * type_mean +
    (slope_animal[animal[ii]] +
       (stype[ii] - 1) * type_slope * type_animal[animal[ii]]) * stimulus[ii] +
    rnorm(n = 1,
          mean = 0,
          sd = extra_error_sd)
}
#convert to binomial
correct_incorrect = rbinom(n = length(response_y),
                           size = 1,
                           prob = plogis(q = response_y - mean(response_y)) )


# Combine this into a single data.frame format object,
# with the experimental design and the measured response data
sim_data = data.frame(
  correct_incorrect = correct_incorrect,
  animal = LETTERS[animal],
  #animal names will now be capital letters
  stimulus = stimulus + 0.001,
  type = factor(stype,
                labels = c('alpha',
                           'beta'))
)
#Inspect data
head(sim_data)
##   correct_incorrect animal stimulus  type
## 1                 0      A    0.001 alpha
## 2                 0      A    1.001 alpha
## 3                 0      A    2.001 alpha
## 4                 1      A    3.001 alpha
## 5                 1      A    4.001 alpha
## 6                 1      A    5.001 alpha

Plot aggregates from the simulated data

dta = sim_data
#Set up plot colours
#on Rstudio these are distinct
clz = sapply(length(unique(dta$animal)),
             colorRampPalette(c(
               'red', 'blue', 'cyan4', 'magenta4', 'orange'
             )))
clz = sample(clz)#Randomise order?

#general overview
#aggragate the proportion correct for each animal
agg = aggregate(correct_incorrect~
                   stimulus * type * animal,
                 data = dta,
                FUN = mean)
#inspect the aggregate values
head(agg)
##   stimulus  type animal correct_incorrect
## 1    0.001 alpha      A              0.00
## 2    1.001 alpha      A              0.00
## 3    2.001 alpha      A              0.00
## 4    3.001 alpha      A              0.65
## 5    4.001 alpha      A              1.00
## 6    5.001 alpha      A              1.00
# open an empty plot
plot(
  NULL,
  xlab = 'Stimulus intensity',
  ylab = 'Proportion correct',
  xlim = range(stimulus) * c(0.7, 1.3),
  ylim = c(0,1),
)
abline(h = c(0,1))
for (aa in agg$animal)
  with(subset(agg, animal == aa),
       #find the subset of the data with this animal
       {
         #Run code using this data as an environment
         points(
           x = stimulus,
           y = correct_incorrect,
           col = clz[which(LETTERS %in% aa)],
           #colour for this animal
           pch = c(20, 21)[1 + type %in% levels(type)[2]]
           # a dot, filled or open
         )
       })
legend(
  x = 'topright',
  legend = unique(agg$animal),
  col = clz,
  pch = 20
)
legend(x = 'bottomright',
       legend = unique(agg$type),
       pch = c(20, 21))

Set up BRMS model

In this model, the correct choices can be predicted from the stimulus intensity, stimulus types and their interaction, as well as individual differences between each animal and their responses to each condition.

frm_brms = bf(correct_incorrect ~
                  stimulus * type +
                  (1 + stimulus * type | animal)
              )

We set some default priors with moderate information. On the logit scale a change in log-odds of 1.0 corresponds to a large change in the probability of an event.

pr_brms = prior("normal(0,1.0)", class = 'b') +
            prior("student_t(3,0,1.0)", class = 'sd')

Run BRMS with rstan

Takes nearly 10 minutes.

system.time({
  mod_rstan = brm(formula = frm_brms,
                  data = dta,
                  prior = pr_brms,
                  family = bernoulli(link = 'logit'),
                  silent = 2,#print only critical messages
                  refresh = 0,
                  chains = 4,
                  cores = 4,#run each chain on a separate CPU
                  iter = 2000,#2000 iterations
                  warmup = 1000,#use the first 1000 to tune the sampler
                  backend = 'rstan'
                  )
})

                  chains = 4,
                  cores = 4,#run each chain on a separate CPU
                  iter = 2000,#2000 iterations
                  warmup = 1000,#use the first 1000 to tune the sampler
                  backend = 'cmdstanr'
                  )
})

Compile BRMS to Stan and run with Nutpie

mod_stan =   make_stancode(formula = frm_brms,
                  data = dta,
                  prior = pr_brms,
                  family = bernoulli(link = 'logit')
                  )
stan_dta = make_standata(formula = frm_brms,
                  data = dta,
                  prior = pr_brms
                  )
# Assign integers the class "integer"
Integerise = function(x) {
  # If it's a numeric vector/scalar and has no decimal parts, make it an integer
  if (is.numeric(x) && all(x == floor(x))) {
    return(as.integer(x))
  }
  return(x)
}

stan_dta  =  lapply(X = stan_dta,
                    FUN = Integerise)

print(mod_stan)
## // generated with brms 2.23.0
## functions {
##  /* compute correlated group-level effects
##   * Args:
##   *   z: matrix of unscaled group-level effects
##   *   SD: vector of standard deviation parameters
##   *   L: cholesky factor correlation matrix
##   * Returns:
##   *   matrix of scaled group-level effects
##   */
##   matrix scale_r_cor(matrix z, vector SD, matrix L) {
##     // r is stored in another dimension order than z
##     return transpose(diag_pre_multiply(SD, L) * z);
##   }
## }
## data {
##   int<lower=1> N;  // total number of observations
##   array[N] int Y;  // response variable
##   int<lower=1> K;  // number of population-level effects
##   matrix[N, K] X;  // population-level design matrix
##   int<lower=1> Kc;  // number of population-level effects after centering
##   // data for group-level effects of ID 1
##   int<lower=1> N_1;  // number of grouping levels
##   int<lower=1> M_1;  // number of coefficients per level
##   array[N] int<lower=1> J_1;  // grouping indicator per observation
##   // group-level predictor values
##   vector[N] Z_1_1;
##   vector[N] Z_1_2;
##   vector[N] Z_1_3;
##   vector[N] Z_1_4;
##   int<lower=1> NC_1;  // number of group-level correlations
##   int prior_only;  // should the likelihood be ignored?
## }
## transformed data {
##   matrix[N, Kc] Xc;  // centered version of X without an intercept
##   vector[Kc] means_X;  // column means of X before centering
##   for (i in 2:K) {
##     means_X[i - 1] = mean(X[, i]);
##     Xc[, i - 1] = X[, i] - means_X[i - 1];
##   }
## }
## parameters {
##   vector[Kc] b;  // regression coefficients
##   real Intercept;  // temporary intercept for centered predictors
##   vector<lower=0>[M_1] sd_1;  // group-level standard deviations
##   matrix[M_1, N_1] z_1;  // standardized group-level effects
##   cholesky_factor_corr[M_1] L_1;  // cholesky factor of correlation matrix
## }
## transformed parameters {
##   matrix[N_1, M_1] r_1;  // actual group-level effects
##   // using vectors speeds up indexing in loops
##   vector[N_1] r_1_1;
##   vector[N_1] r_1_2;
##   vector[N_1] r_1_3;
##   vector[N_1] r_1_4;
##   // prior contributions to the log posterior
##   real lprior = 0;
##   // compute actual group-level effects
##   r_1 = scale_r_cor(z_1, sd_1, L_1);
##   r_1_1 = r_1[, 1];
##   r_1_2 = r_1[, 2];
##   r_1_3 = r_1[, 3];
##   r_1_4 = r_1[, 4];
##   lprior += normal_lpdf(b | 0,1.0);
##   lprior += student_t_lpdf(Intercept | 3, 0, 2.5);
##   lprior += student_t_lpdf(sd_1 | 3,0,1.0)
##     - 4 * student_t_lccdf(0 | 3,0,1.0);
##   lprior += lkj_corr_cholesky_lpdf(L_1 | 1);
## }
## model {
##   // likelihood including constants
##   if (!prior_only) {
##     // initialize linear predictor term
##     vector[N] mu = rep_vector(0.0, N);
##     mu += Intercept;

##     }
##     target += bernoulli_logit_glm_lpmf(Y | Xc, mu, b);
##   }
##   // priors including constants
##   target += lprior;
##   target += std_normal_lpdf(to_vector(z_1));

## generated quantities {
##   // actual population-level intercept

##   // compute group-level correlations
##   corr_matrix[M_1] Cor_1 = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_1);
##   vector<lower=-1,upper=1>[NC_1] cor_1;
##   // extract upper diagonal of correlation matrix
##   for (k in 1:M_1) {
##     for (j in 1:(k - 1)) {
##       cor_1[choose(k - 1, 2) + j] = Cor_1[j, k];
##     }
##   }
## }

Takes around 3 minutes.

system.time({
# Compile Stan code
compiled_nutstan = nutpie$compile_stan_model(code = mod_stan)

# Use do.call to unpack the R list into arguments for the Python method
compiled_nutstan = do.call(what = compiled_nutstan$with_data,
                           args =  stan_dta)

mod_nutpie_stan = nutpie$sample(compiled_nutstan,
                                draws = 1000L,       # 1000L forces R to pass it as a long count integer
                                tune = 1000L)   #use the first 1000 to tune the sampler
})
##    user  system elapsed 
## 930.434   7.101 190.817
plt = import("matplotlib.pyplot")
az$summary(mod_nutpie_stan,
           var_names = c('Intercept',
                         'b')
          )[, c(1, 3, 4, 7, 9)]
##             mean hdi_3% hdi_97% ess_bulk r_hat
## Intercept -1.412 -3.771   0.719     1464  1.01
## b[0]       2.312  1.621   2.950     2059  1.00
## b[1]       0.830 -0.740   2.423     2315  1.00
## b[2]       2.818  1.758   3.906     2437  1.00
aplot = az$plot_trace(mod_nutpie_stan,
              var_names = c('Intercept',
                         'b'))
plt$show()

Everything fits well, but coefficient names (default Stan names) are not very easy to interpret.

Run Bambi with Nutpie

# Import the necessary Python modules
bmb = import("bambi")


# Set up the priors using R lists parsed into Bambi Priors
bambi_priors = list(
  "common" = bmb$Prior("Normal", mu = 0, sigma = 1.0),
  "group"  = bmb$Prior("HalfStudentT", mu = 0, sigma = 1.0, nu = 3)
)

# Pull the R objects cleanly into the Python environment
py$py_data <- dta
py$bambi_priors <- bambi_priors

Takes around 120 seconds!

system.time({
  
py_run_string("
import bambi as bmb
bmb_model = bmb.Model(
    formula = 'correct_incorrect ~ stimulus * type + (1 + stimulus * type | animal)',
    data = py_data,
    family = 'bernoulli',
    priors = bambi_priors,
    center_predictors = False
)
")

# Fit using the nutpie engine
mod_nutpie_bambi = py$bmb_model$fit(
    draws=1000L,
    tune=1000L,
    nuts_sampler="nutpie"
)
})
##    user  system elapsed 
## 200.393   3.068  70.045

In Bambi coefficients have intuitive names linked to the predictor variable names. But some divergences appear that were not present for the Stan model. It is possible that the default parametrisation in Bambi is less stable. This could easily be addressed by using target_adapt = 0.95 for smaller sampling steps. (possibly also center_predictors = False in bmb.Model)

az$summary(mod_nutpie_bambi,
           var_names = c('Intercept',
                          'stimulus',
                         'type',
                         '1|animal_sigma')
          )[, c(1, 3, 4, 7, 9)]
##                  mean hdi_3% hdi_97% ess_bulk r_hat
## Intercept      -1.763 -3.707   0.081     2624  1.00
## stimulus        2.120  1.500   2.796     1359  1.01
## type[beta]      0.255 -1.334   1.748     4437  1.00
## 1|animal_sigma  7.985  5.682  10.202     1549  1.00
aplot = az$plot_trace(mod_nutpie_bambi,
              var_names = c('Intercept',
                          'stimulus',
                         'type',
                         '1|animal_sigma')
              )
plt$show()

Summary

Ultimately it looks like the fastest and easiest way to sample a GLMM is to use Nutpie via Bambi. But beware of awkward reticulate issues! It is not straightforward to get R and Python environments aligned and talking to each other.
